tex_content.html:
Lemma
[A surjection splits its domain]

Let $A : E \to E'$ be a surjective linear map of finite-dimensional real vector spaces and let $P : E \to \ker A$ be a linear projection onto $\ker A$. Then $v \mapsto (Av, Pv)$ is a linear isomorphism $E \cong E' \times \ker A$.

Proof

Injectivity: if $Av = 0$ and $Pv = 0$, then $v \in \ker A$, and $P$ restricts to the identity on $\ker A$, so $v = Pv = 0$. Surjectivity: given $(u,k) \in E' \times \ker A$, pick $w$ with $Aw = u$ and set $v = w - Pw + k$. Since $Pw$ and $k$ lie in $\ker A$, $Av = Aw = u$; and $P$ is the identity on $\ker A$, so $Pv = Pw - Pw + k = k$. A projection onto $\ker A$ exists because every subspace of a finite-dimensional space is complemented, and it is continuous because every linear map out of a finite-dimensional space is.

□
